# Test-Time Scaling in Reasoning LLMs: Inference Regimes, Evaluation, and Reproducibility

- **Authors**: Mohsen Hariri, Weicong Chen, Nahal Shahini, Vikash Singh, Kai Ye, Amirhossein Samandar, Debargha Ganguly, Sreehari Sankar, Yanyan Zhang, Shouren Wang, Jerry Peng, Biyao Zhang, Michael Hinczewski, Vipin Chaudhary
- **Venue**: cs.LG
- **Published**: 2026-08-04
- **Source**: arxiv
- **Link**: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.04001>
- **PDF**: <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.04001v1>
- **Topics**: test-time-scaling
- **Relevance score**: reasoning-faithfulness 0.25, test-time-scaling 0.57

## In one line

Formalizes test-time scaling as budgeted inference over a model's implicit prefix tree, separates three structurally different regimes that a single scalar budget conflates, specifies what a reproducible inference protocol must declare, and releases 1.9 million traces — with the empirical section showing a selection score that makes accuracy fall from 75.56% to 65.83% as the candidate bank grows.

## Problem

The phrase test-time scaling now covers algorithms with different statistical structure, compute accounting and failure modes: extending one trajectory, sampling completed candidates and reducing them by voting or verification, and searching over unfinished partial states. Reporting them under a single scalar budget, or reporting accuracy without the inference protocol that produced it, makes results incomparable across papers. Evaluation is correspondingly harder than benchmarking a checkpoint, because measured performance depends on the whole protocol — prompt template, decoder, search controller, reducer, verifier, stopping rule and numerical settings — and even with prompts and methods fixed, estimates vary from stochastic decoding and implementation details.

## Contributions

- A taxonomy grounded in where compute is spent on the prefix tree: single-trajectory sequential scaling with no competing frontier, leaf-level scaling with a terminal reducer over completed candidates, and prefix-level scaling that allocates on scores for unfinished states
- Treating the evaluated object as the entire inference system, and separating a shared-bank comparison — which isolates aggregation given one completed candidate pool — from end-to-end evaluation of the complete system
- Modelling causal stopping separately from evidence extraction and selection, on the exact ground that only stopping can reduce generation cost, since the others act after the traces they read are already complete
- A discovery-stability profile from which the common repeated-sampling metrics are recovered as coordinates or simple functionals — pass@k, pass^k, majority-vote lower bounds, G-Pass@k and its averaged form — with finite-bank and Bayesian variants
- A reproducibility specification distinguishing exact replay from distributional reproducibility, and naming the artifacts each requires
- A released corpus of 1,948,821 reasoning traces across 22,449 questions in four blocks with progressively richer verifier and token-level signals

## Method

The formalization writes a budgeted algorithm over the implicit prefix tree induced by generation, with a local decoding policy inducing a proposal distribution over completed leaves that may differ from the raw model distribution. Reduction rules are catalogued as instances of one expected-utility template — verifier-constrained selection, answer marginalization and self-consistency shown to be empirical minimum-Bayes-risk with agreement utility, learned reranking, and general utility selection. For stopping, across-rollout and within-rollout stopping times are given measurability conditions stating exactly what information each may use, so that an online claim can only be supported by a causally faithful retrospective replay. Compute accounting decomposes total cost into generation and evaluation, the latter into signal, control and decision, and notes that equal sample counts need not imply equal compute. The empirical study fixes response banks so new reducers can be evaluated without regenerating anything, over four blocks: one-response coverage across 27 open-weight reasoning models on broad knowledge and symbolic reasoning, and 80-response banks on competition mathematics with exact without-replacement bank statistics and reducers replayed on nested random subsets of the same banks — so differences among reducers cannot be attributed to newly generated candidates.

## Results

The empirical section is a set of measurements about candidate banks rather than a method comparison, and three are worth carrying. Discovery and consistency move in opposite directions with budget: across 20 configurations the median chance of at least one correct candidate rises from 56.49% at one sample to 82.08% at eighty, while the median chance that *all* drawn candidates are correct falls to 15.00% — on the strongest configuration, 91.67% against 43.33%. So a rising pass@k curve is compatible with within-question stability collapsing, and reporting only the first hides the second. Second, ranking is nearly settled at small budgets: mean Spearman agreement with the eighty-sample accuracy ordering is 0.967 at one sample and 0.992 at eight, which bounds how much a large-budget sweep buys for model comparison specifically. Third, and sharpest, more compute can lower submitted accuracy when the selection score is misaligned with correctness — selecting by mean token log probability falls from 75.56% at one sample to 65.83% at eighty on the strongest configuration, while literal answer plurality rises to 78.33% and sequence log-probability selection reaches 77.50% on the same banks. The paper also reports its reference-assisted verifier at 89.17% and flags immediately that it sees the gold answer and is not an inference-time result, which is the kind of labelling this archive usually has to supply itself.

## Limitations

The paper is a formalization and a resource rather than a claim about which method is best, and it says so throughout — the empirical numbers are described as descriptive properties of the specific configurations measured, not as general small-sample guarantees. What a reader should hold: the taxonomy's regimes are explicitly not mutually exclusive, since most practical systems are hybrids of prefix search followed by a leaf-level reducer, so classifying a real system still requires judgement. The repeated-sampling diagnostics have their independent-attempt interpretation only when the bank comes from independent draws of a declared fixed proposal; for banks produced by adaptive search or dependent procedures they remain descriptive summaries of what was returned, which the paper states and which most papers reporting pass@k do not. The released banks are large but fixed, so any reducer evaluated on them inherits whatever the generating protocols produced. And the prescriptions — protocol-consistent uncertainty propagated through the aggregation rule, declaration of budget, temperature, evidence map, stopping and extraction rules before outcomes are inspected — are normative requirements the paper argues for rather than empirical findings, and it does not measure how often current work violates them.

## Why it matters here

- **test-time-scaling**: This is the vocabulary this archive has been missing, and it supplies precise names for confusions the archive has been recording one paper at a time. Its three regimes explain why results in this archive have been hard to pool: a budget-forcing method, a best-of-N selector and a tree search are not three settings of one knob. Its insistence that the evaluated object is the whole inference system — checkpoint, prompt, decoder, controller, reducer, verifier, budget and stopping rule — is the general form of the archive's baseline-validity finding, and its shared-bank versus end-to-end distinction is the general form of the selector-matched controls the archive has praised in two separate papers. Three specific things transfer immediately. The observation that only causal stopping can save generation cost, because extraction and fixed-bank selection act on traces already complete, is a compute-accounting rule the archive's efficiency papers should be read against. The discovery-stability profile makes pass@k, pass^k and majority-vote bounds coordinates of one object, which is why the archive's reasoning-boundary dispute could be argued to opposite conclusions with different coordinates of the same profile. And the mean-log-probability reducer declining from 75.56% to 65.83% as the bank grows is a third independent instance of this archive's finding that sampling more is not monotone — the cleanest yet, because the bank is fixed and only the reducer varies, so nothing but the selection rule can explain it.

## Abstract

Large language models can solve substantially harder reasoning problems with more inference-time compute. The term "test-time scaling," however, now covers diverse inference algorithms that extend deliberation along a single trajectory, sample completed candidates and aggregate them through voting or verification, or search over unfinished partial states. These algorithms differ in their statistical structure, compute accounting, and failure modes. Treating these procedures as interchangeable under a single scalar "budget," or reporting accuracy without the inference protocol that produced it, makes results difficult to compare across studies. We develop a systematic account of test-time scaling along three axes. First, we formalize test-time scaling as budgeted inference over the implicit prefix tree of an autoregressive model and distinguish three structural regimes: single-trajectory sequential scaling, leaf-level scaling with terminal reduction, and prefix-level scaling. Second, we treat the evaluated object as the entire inference system and develop evaluation principles that separate end-to-end system performance from candidate-bank diagnostics. We introduce an evaluation profile whose coordinates and simple functionals recover or bound common repeated-sampling metrics, and prescribe protocol-matched reporting of compute and uncertainty. Third, we specify reproducibility requirements for inference protocols, distinguishing exact replay from distributional reproducibility and identifying the artifacts needed to support each. We also organize the open-weight reasoning ecosystem by model-side and interface mechanisms, apply these principles to broad-knowledge, symbolic-reasoning, and competition-mathematics benchmarks, and assemble over 2 billion full reasoning traces for release with progressively richer verifier and token-level signals.
